paper_title: When Fine-Grained Credit Assignment Helps and Hurts: Multimodal Agentic Reinforcement Learning through Video Editing

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise for training multimodal agents to reason and use tools. However, it remains unclear when fine-grained credit assignment improves learning and when it fails to improve task performance. Video editing provides a useful testbed for this question, combining multimodal perception, long-horizon planning, and tool use with delayed outcome feedback. We construct four movie-trailer editing task types---Content Selection, Narrative Sequencing, Rough Cut, and Fine Cut---that reflect real-world editing workflows and span different levels of task complexity and interaction horizon. Decaying process rewards provides the largest benefit on Fine Cut, with a 45.4% relative gain over outcome-only GRPO on tasks averaging more than 60 turns under outcome-only GRPO. On the three shorter-horizon task types averaging 30--40 turns under the same baseline, outcome-only GRPO remains competitive, with decaying process rewards yielding at most a 10.4% relative gain. Process rewards from an LLM judge initially improve tool use and encourage visual inspection. As training progresses, however, GRPO+PRM with a fixed process-reward weight increasingly exhibits excessive reasoning and redundant tool calls: process rewards continue to rise while task completion rates and outcome scores decline. Decaying the process-reward weight to zero mitigates this reward-hacking behavior while preserving the early gains. Despite dense token-level supervision, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) yields little improvement or substantial degradation and is highly sensitive to the choice of privileged information. Our analysis reveals differences in teacher--student disagreement and gradient magnitudes, and suggests possible dilution of informative signals over long trajectories.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Video agents are moving from video understanding towards long-horizon multimodal tasks such as video production, where models must integrate multimodal perception, planning, and tool use (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Sandoval-Castañeda et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b). However, even the strongest agent systems struggle on these tasks (Cao et al., 2026; Hu et al., Part of this work was completed while Lei Zhao was an intern at Philo Labs. Shading marks the decayed variants 2030 decay window. 2026). Reinforcement learning has shown promise for improving their performance, enabling agents to refine their decision-making and tool-use policies through feedback from task execution (Kulkarni and Fazli, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2025d). However, reward formulation remains challenging because the quality of the resulting video rests on subjective judgment (Yan et al., 2026a; Wen et al., 2026). In addition, feedback on the final video becomes available only after sequence of interdependent editing decisions, making it difficult to determine how individual actions contribute to the final outcome. Credit assignment is therefore central to training these agents (Arjona-Medina et al., 2019; Feng et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2026). 2 Yet it remains unclear when finer-grained credit assignment helps or hurts learning in long-horizon multimodal tasks. Most work on video production builds workflow around model that it never updates (SandovalCastañeda et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b). Crayotter trains an editing agent with segment-level credit, where segments group consecutive editing events from the same stage (Yan et al., 2026a). We ask how trajectory-, turn-, and token-level credit compare across editing tasks under shared training setup. Elsewhere, several lines report that finer credit helps. VAGEN gives multi-turn visual agent dense turn-level supervision (Wang et al., 2025b), TAPO repairs the credit that trajectory-level advantage misassigns to tool calls inside failed rollouts (Dong et al., 2026), and interface agents trained on step-level progress signals beat actors trained on outcome rewards alone (Zhang et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025). Other work reports negative results for process rewards. Group-relative optimization with an outcome reward provably carries an implicit process reward, which makes an explicit one look redundant (Sullivan and Koller, 2025). process reward is dense but remains prone to bias and reward hacking (Zheng et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026). Outcome-only training is argued to suffice on long horizons once exploration is wide enough (Pu et al., 2026). How credit should be assigned in long-horizon multimodal agents therefore remains unclear. We study the question in movie-trailer editing. We generate 797 tasks from 49 real movies and their released trailers. The work decomposes into four stages that human editor performs in order, which give the task types Content Selection (CS), Narrative Sequencing (NS), Rough Cut (RC), and Fine Cut (FC). The four types differ in editing requirements, interaction length, and in the quality profile of the turns they elicit, which lets us ask how the same credit signal behaves as the task changes. We train Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) for 50 updates on 716 of these tasks under four schemes that cover the three granularities. At the trajectory level we use outcome-only GRPO. At the turn level we compare GRPO+PRM (fixed λ) and GRPO+PRM (decayed λ). Both use process reward from Gemini 3.8 Flash, averaged over three votes. At the token level we use on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). Its teacher receives privileged information that the student never sees: reference answers or turn-level suggestions. Outcome scores come from Gemini 3.1 Pro, so the process reward and the outcome reward never share model. The schemes share the base model, training tasks, and number of updates, while objective-specific settings are detailed in Appendix C.1. We evaluate every run on 81 validation tasks four times and report the mean, and we record how the agent behaves as well as what it scores. Our contributions are threefold. First, we develop data-construction pipeline that turns films and their released trailers into four types of editing tasks reflecting real-world editing workflows. Training on these tasks improves Qwen3.5-9Bs video editing performance on held-out films. Second, we compare trajectory-, turn-, and token-level learning signals under shared setup. Decaying process rewards yields 45.4% relative gain over outcome-only GRPO on Fine Cut, while outcomeonly GRPO remains competitive on the three shorter-horizon task types. Third, we analyze training dynamics and model behavior to identify limitations of the tested finer-grained signals: fixed process rewards can undermine task completion despite encouraging desirable behaviors, and OPSD is sensitive to the privileged information provided to its teacher.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Agents for video production. Video-editing agents have evolved from executing languageguided actions to managing long-horizon multi-stage production (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Sandoval-Castañeda et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025c; Ding et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026c; Zhang et al., 2026b; Liang et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2026b; Zhou et al., 2026a). These systems focus on designing editing workflows while keeping the underlying models fixed. Despite this progress, advanced agents remain unreliable in professional video post-production tasks (Cao et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026). Another line of work trains video-editing policies (Tang et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2026b; Yu et al., 2026). These methods use policy gradients for shot composition or supervised and preference-based post-training for tool-using planners. Crayotter assigns segment-level credit based on rankings of finished videos produced for the same task (Yan et al., 2026a). Our study compares trajectory-, turn-, and token-level supervision across shared suite of editing tasks. Credit assignment for long-horizon agents. Attributing delayed outcomes to the decisions that caused them is long-standing challenge (Arjona-Medina et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2021; Harutyunyan et al., 2019; Mesnard et al., 2020; Meulemans et al., 2023). Research on language agents builds explicit learning signals at several granularities. Trajectory-level methods score whole rollout against its peers (Shao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025d). Turn-level methods estimate value, progress, or relative advantage for each turn (Zhou et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a; Feng et al., 2025; Xi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Tan et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). Finer methods assign an advantage to reasoning step or segment within response (Kazemnejad et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). Multimodal work follows the same three levels across visual, interface, embodied, and video agents (Wang et al., 2025b; Pang et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhou et al., 2026c; Xu et al., 2025; Kulkarni and Fazli, 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c). Whether explicit finer-grained supervision improves learning remains an empirical question. Under mild assumptions, outcome-only GRPO can be written as process-aware objective that carries an implicit Monte Carlo process reward (Sullivan and Koller, 2025). Process reward models are also hard to build and to evaluate. Synthesizing their labels by Monte Carlo estimation generalizes worse than using judge or human annotator (Zhang et al., 2025b), and benchmarks for fine-grained error detection expose substantial weaknesses in current models (Song et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026). Empirical studies nevertheless report benefits from denser feedback (Wang and Ammanabrolu, 2025; Wu et al., 2026), alongside failure modes involving teacher guidance, reward-model overoptimization, and proxy exploitation (Li et al., 2026d; Fu et al., 2026; Skalse et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2023; Thaman, 2026; Pu et al., 2026; Gunjal et al., 2026; Shao et al., 2025). Evidence remains limited on when finer-grained supervision helps or hurts long-horizon multimodal agents, and how these effects vary across tasks and training stages.

sections.title: 4.1 Tasks and Environment
sections.content: We study movie-trailer editing as it is done in practice (Murch, 2001; Pearlman, 2012). We decompose the editing of one trailer into four stages that human editor works through in order, following the workflow-oriented view of AgenticVBench (Cao et al., 2026). Each stage gives one task type, namely Content Selection (CS), Narrative Sequencing (NS), Rough Cut (RC), and Fine Cut (FC). Figure 1(a) illustrates the four editing operations. task consists of multi-turn episode in which the agent inspects the supplied media and commits its artifact. The released trailer provides reference answer for each task, held by the evaluator and hidden from the agent. Table 1 gives the task, the input, and the output of each type of task. See Appendix for the definition of each type and Appendix A.7 for two worked examples. Base scores range from 0.152 to 0.657 under the respective task metrics, and mean interaction horizons range from 15.3 to 87.2 turns. Scoring. Each task is scored on the artifact the agent commits when the episode ends. All tasks use the same three channels for this outcome score Rout, Rout = wdetRdet + wref Rref + wblindRblind, (4.1) where Rdet is deterministic verifier that scores the artifact against that reference answer, Rref is multimodal LLM judge that scores the artifact with that reference, and Rblind is the same judge asking whether the artifact works on its own terms. Both judge channels score against weighted rubric, and one model call grades each rubric item with its own evidence attached. The weights of Equation 4.1 sum to one and vary with the type. In this paper, we use Gemini 3.1 Pro as the multimodal LLM judge. The process rewards used during training come from different model. Content Selection and Narrative Sequencing use only the deterministic score, with weights (1, 0, 0). Content Selection scores the unordered selected shot set against the reference set using F1, 2S S/(S + S). It evaluates selection alone, with partial credit for overlap.1 Narrative Sequencing scores agreement with the reference order. Rough Cut uses (0.4, 0.4, 0.2), combining deterministic cut-point similarity with reference-conditioned and reference-free judge scores. Fine Cut uses (0, 0.4, 0.6) to assess sound design and transitions through the two judge channels. These task-specific metrics measure different editing objectives, so their absolute values are not common scale of task difficulty. Each task runs in fresh workspace holding the editorial brief, manifest, and the media the task type exposes. The agent is provided with shell and eight media tools for inspecting pictures, probing audio, and validating its own artifact. See Appendix B.2 for the full list. sections.title: 4.2 Data Construction and Dataset
sections.content: Given source film and its released trailer, we detect shot boundaries and align usable trailer shots to their source-film footage. We partition the trailer into narratively coherent chunks and generate an editorial brief for each, describing its narrative role without identifying the clips. Each chunk yields one task of each type by varying the supplied media and required editing operation  (Table 1)  . Figure 2 illustrates the pipeline, and Appendix gives the construction details. The pipeline produces 2,352 tasks from 49 films. After filtering with Gemini 3.8 Flash we sample 797 of them, 716 for training from 43 films and 81 for validation from 6 films that do not appear in training. Table 2 gives the split by task type, and Appendix lists the films and describes the audit and the sampling protocol. Table 2: Task counts by type. The training and validation films are disjoint.

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Training settings. We train Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) for 50 updates on the 716 training tasks (Section 4.2) under four different schemes for credit assignment: (i) outcome-only GRPO, (ii) GRPO+PRM (fixed λ), (iii) GRPO+PRM (decayed λ), and (iv) OPSD. For GRPO+PRM (fixed λ), we use process-reward weight of λ = 0.5 throughout training. GRPO+PRM (decayed λ) keeps the same weight until update 20. We then decay it to zero over updates 2030 and keep it at zero thereafter. Section 6.2 explains the choice of this interval, and Appendix gives the decay schedule and full training configuration. For OPSD, we compare two forms of privileged information: reference answers and turn-level suggestions. Gemini 3.8 Flash generates the turn-level suggestions from the students context at each turn. These suggestions are provided to the frozen teacher as privileged information. Evaluation. We evaluate the final checkpoint of each run on the 81 validation tasks introduced in Section 4.2. To reduce evaluation variance, we evaluate every task four times and report the mean score, denoted avg@4. See Appendix for the full evaluation configuration.

sections.title: 5.2 Experiment Results
sections.content: Table 3 summarizes the results. Outcome-only GRPO improves all four task types, raising the overall score from 0.284 to 0.413. Unexpectedly, GRPO+PRM (fixed λ) scores lower than outcome-only GRPO on every task type except Fine Cut. Decaying the process-reward weight improves all four task scores over GRPO+PRM (fixed λ) and yields the highest overall score of 0.447. Its largest gain over outcome-only GRPO is on Fine Cut (0.293 vs. 0.201). OPSD (reference answers) performs similarly to the untrained model (0.277 vs. 0.284 overall), while OPSD (turn-level suggestions) drops to 0.044. Section 6 analyzes these contrasting outcomes.

sections.title: 6 Credit Assignment: Benefits and Failure Modes
sections.content: We examine trajectory-level credit on long horizons in Section 6.1. Section 6.2 links process-reward hacking to declining task completion and studies process-reward weight decay as mitigation. Section 6.3 examines the sensitivity of OPSD to privileged information.

sections.title: 6.2 GRPO+PRM: Reward Hacking and Mitigation
sections.content: Reward hacking with fixed process-reward weight. All task types except Fine Cut score lower than outcome-only GRPO, as shown in Table 3. Table 5 further shows sharp decline in the models ability to deliver result, with 44.1% of rollouts being truncated compared with only 0.3% under outcome-only GRPO. Late in training, the model continues calling tools to gather evidence but often stops before committing to final result. We further analyze the training dynamics of GRPO+PRM (fixed λ). As shown in Figure 1(c), the process reward increases while the outcome reward declines after update 30. Appendix C.7 provides 9 Table 4: Turn-level quality of the untrained models rollouts from the second evaluation repetition on all 81 validation tasks, scored by the process-reward judge. Task type Positive Neutral Negative Mixing CS NS RC FC 55.3% 42.7% 44.5% 16.7% 36.0% 44.9% 43.6% 47.5% 8.7% 0.297 12.4% 0.355 0.390 11.9% 35.8% 0.651 the full training curves. As shown in Section 7, process rewards encourage desirable behaviors such as visual inspection, reasoning, and reflection. One possible interpretation is that encouraging these behaviors helps improve task scores early in training. Later, continued optimization with fixed process-reward weight may lead the model to overuse these behaviors, consuming its interaction budget and reducing its ability to complete the task. Process-reward weight decay mitigates reward hacking. Observations in Figure 1(c) motivate us to decay the process-reward weight λ to zero between updates 20 and 30. This schedule retains process guidance early in training and shifts later updates to the outcome reward alone. Results in Table 3 show that this approach is effective. On the first three task types, the model achieves performance comparable to outcome-only GRPO, with an average score of 0.568 versus 0.559. On Fine Cut, the method improves performance over the untrained model by 0.141, whereas outcome-only GRPO yields an improvement of only 0.050. As shown in Section 7, decaying the process-reward weight further encourages desirable behaviors, such as longer reasoning and more frequent reflection, compared with keeping the weight fixed.

sections.title: 6.3 OPSD Is Sensitive to Privileged information
sections.content: With reference answers, OPSD scores 0.277, close to the untrained models 0.284. With turn-level suggestions, its score drops to 0.044  (Table 3)  . OPSD gradients depend on privileged information. The two variants share the same distillation loss, frozen teacher, student model, and training hyperparameters. Compared with reference answers, turn-level suggestions yield an approximately 15-fold larger mean forward KL divergence and increase the mean gradient norm from 0.084 to 1.177  (Table 13)  . The OPSD signal can be diluted over trajectory. With reference answers, the most divergent 5% of turns account for 47.4% of the total KL but only 17.9% of the tokens  (Table 14)  . This concentration suggests that averaging over valid assistant tokens may dilute the contribution of the more divergent turns. However, KL measures disagreement rather than the usefulness of teacher guidance, and whether gradient magnitude or signal dilution causes the observed outcomes remains to be tested. Appendix C.5 provides further analysis of trajectory lengths, gradient norms, and KL concentration.

Process rewards encourage desirable behaviors but do not ensure completion. Compared with outcome-only GRPO, GRPO+PRM (fixed λ) encourages more visual inspection, longer reasoning, and more frequent self-correction markers  (Table 5)  . However, these changes accompany higher scores only on Fine Cut; scores fall on the other three task types  (Table 3)  . The truncation rate also rises from 0.3% to 44.1%. The value of these behaviors therefore depends on the task and on whether the model can still complete it. GRPO gains accompany greater visual inspection. Compared with the base model, outcomeonly GRPO increases frames seen from 32.2 to 84.2, without increasing tool calls or reasoning length  (Table 5)  . Greater visual input may help the three shorter-horizon tasks, consistent with their larger gains, whereas Fine Cut may require more complex tool use and reasoning to coordinate longer sequence of editing operations. Less process guidance mitigates hacking and elicits better behavioral patterns. Compared with GRPO+PRM (fixed λ), GRPO+PRM (decayed λ) makes fewer tool calls while retaining substantial visual inspection, producing longer reasoning, and showing more frequent self-correction markers  (Table 5)  . These changes accompany reduction in truncation from 44.1% to 6.2% and an 11 increase in overall task score from 0.334 to 0.447  (Table 3)  . Compared with outcome-only GRPO, GRPO+PRM (decayed λ) achieves substantial gain on Fine Cut, which may be associated with its longer reasoning and more extensive visual inspection. OPSD behavior depends on privileged information. As shown in Table 5, with reference answers, OPSD remains behaviorally close to the untrained model, apart from lower blind rate. With turn-level suggestions, rollouts become much shorter, reasoning length and reflection frequency drop sharply, and blind rollouts become more frequent. These behavioral changes accompany the collapse in task performance  (Table 3)  .

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: Our experiments show when finer-grained credit helps and when it hurts. Process guidance helps most on Fine Cut, while outcome-only GRPO remains competitive on shorter-horizon tasks. Process guidance can hurt when more visual inspection and reasoning accompany poorer task completion. Decaying the process-reward weight improves completion while retaining these behaviors. OPSD is sensitive to privileged information, showing that dense supervision alone does not guarantee effective learning. Our process-reward findings are based on GRPO+PRM with LLM-judged turnlevel rewards on movie-trailer editing tasks; whether they extend to untested methods such as GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) and Turn-PPO (Li et al., 2026b) remains open. For OPSD, we identify failure patterns without establishing effective remedies. How to improve teacher guidance and training stability requires further study.

sections.content: Figure 2 gives an overview of the data generation pipeline. A.1 Corpus and Summary Statistics Let Dedit = {(Fi, Ti)}N where Fi is source film and Ti is its corresponding trailer. The corpus contains = 49 pairs, comprising 101.80 hours of source video and 2.09 hours of trailers. Instantiating four task types for every retained chunk produces an initial pool of 2,352 tasks, before task-level quality filtering and sampling. The final experimental dataset contains 797 tasks (Section 4.2). (A.1) i=1, A.2 Media Processing and Chunking Task construction converts each long film and short trailer into localized editing problems. We normalize media geometry and create analysis proxies, then detect shot boundaries in both videos. coarse-to-fine visual matching pipeline aligns trailer shots to candidate source-film moments and rejects low-confidence matches. Graphic cards, black frames, flashes, and other featureless intervals are separated from usable footage. Speech timestamps, music activity, and picturesound relations are extracted only for constructing fine-cut tasks and hidden evaluation evidence; the finished trailer mix and its alignments are never exposed to the policy. semantic pass groups the trailer into broad story beats and then into local chunks that do not cross beat boundaries. The construction produces 622 raw chunks. We retain 588 chunks containing at least three usable picture clips and two source-film anchors. The source films contain 88,669 detected shots and the trailers contain 5,978 detected shots. A.3 Construction by Task Type The four tasks for chunk are constructed independently. Narrative Sequencing uses the reference selection, Rough Cut uses the reference order, and Fine Cut starts from reference rough cut rather than sampled upstream output. This prevents one task types errors from dominating another task types training signal. The corpus therefore evaluates stagewise editing decisions; composing all task types into fully end-to-end trailer editor is separate setting. Content Selection presents complete source shots rather than pre-trimmed positives and mixes them with neighboring and duration-matched distractors. In the final dataset, each task contains 2136 candidates and 314 positives. Narrative Sequencing independently renames and shuffles the selected clips. Overlapping neighboring source windows are separated where possible so that the task cannot be solved by matching duplicate boundary frames. Rough Cut supplies the reference order but requires new inand out-points for every clip. Matching ambiguity is retained as timing tolerance, avoiding frame-exact penalties when equivalent boundaries exist. Fine Cut begins from stable rough cut and exposes production-sound handles, uncut dialogue candidates, an unaligned music window, and join metadata. The agent selects and trims dialogue, places music, chooses picture and sound transitions, and renders the result. Trailer-only picture is muted so that released dialogue and music choices cannot be recovered from its audio. The structured edit and rendered preview are evaluated together. 19 Figure 2: Data generation from filmtrailer pair. (a) Two real source clips and their referencealigned cuts illustrate shot matching. (b) Each local chunk stays within story beat and receives clip-independent brief. (c) Four tasks share the brief and initialize from reference states, so errors in sampled outputs cannot propagate between tasks. Timeline and asset layouts are schematic. D/M/S denote dialogue, music, and production sound. 20 A.4 Task Inputs, Outputs, and Requirements Each task package provides local editing brief, the assets under initial_state/, and public manifest.json describing those assets. The manifest identifies files and their local time coordinates; it is not an answer key. Hidden selections, reference orders, sourcetrailer alignments, and grading references are kept outside the policy-visible package. The four interfaces expose different decisions, as detailed below. Their scores use different criteria and should not be interpreted as common difficulty scale. Content Selection (CS): choose an unordered subset. The input is written description of the local trailer stretch and pool of complete, silent source shots, with candidate IDs, file names, and durations in the manifest. Positive shots are mixed with distractors from the same film. Candidate numbering follows shuffle and does not indicate relevance. The agent must screen the pool and decide both which clips to keep and how many to keep. It writes output/selection.json, containing selected array of candidate IDs. Each selected ID is listed once; the order of IDs has no meaning. The task does not ask the agent to rank the candidates, order the selected shots, choose temporal boundaries, mix audio, or render video. The score is the set-selection F1 against the hidden selection: precision is the fraction of selected valid candidates that belong to the reference set, and recall is the fraction of reference candidates selected. An empty selection receives zero. The reference selection size is not supplied and is not submission constraint; selecting too many clips is penalized through precision and selecting too few through recall. This is continuous F1 score, not binary task-success rate. The task grader additionally reports missed and incorrect clips; its diagnostic pass flag is separate from the reported score. Narrative Sequencing (NS): order the supplied shots. The input contains the referenceselected shots, independently shuffled and renamed, together with description of the desired narrative stretch. Unlike the silent CS pool, the NS clips include production sound. The agent can use action continuity, dialogue, eyelines, movement, shot size, scene changes, and the brief to recover an ordering. It writes output/order.json, whose order array lists every supplied ID exactly once, from first to last. Dropping shot, duplicating an ID, or introducing new ID is invalid. The agent does not choose subset, trim shots, or alter the sound mix. The deterministic score combines three complementary properties of the permutation: one minus normalized positional displacement, the normalized longest increasing subsequence, and the fraction of directed reference-adjacent pairs retained. These three factors are multiplied. Thus, preserving some pairwise order alone does not ensure that the sequence preserves the reference joins. The Heretic chunk 5 grader used in our experiments accepts four explicitly enumerated orders and takes the best match among them; this is task-specific repair rather than general acceptance of arbitrary alternative orders. Rough Cut (RC): choose an interval within every ordered clip. The input supplies the selected clips in their reference order, their available durations, local editing brief, and target total duration. The agent writes output/cuts.json. Each object in its cuts array contains clip, in_s, and out_s. Times are measured from the beginning of the named source clip, rather than on global film or output timeline. All supplied clips must appear exactly once and in the supplied order. Every kept interval must have nonnegative start, an end after its start, and boundaries within the available media. The sum of the kept durations must stay near the supplied target. The agent chooses where an action begins and ends and how much time each shot receives; it does not reselect or reorder the material, add dialogue, or redesign the mix. The grading pipeline renders the submitted cuts for evaluation. The final RC score combines deterministic timing component (weight 0.4), reference-informed judgment (0.4), and judgment without the reference (0.2). The deterministic component is the fraction of scorable shots for which both the in-point error and the kept-duration error are within their reference tolerances. In-point tolerances are specific to each shot, reflecting matching ambiguity; they are not universal frame-exact threshold. Shots with no source-film counterpart remain part of the required sequence but are excluded from this timing-component denominator. Submission validity and the full judging rubrics are detailed in Appendix C. Fine Cut (FC): finish sound and transitions on fixed picture edit. The input is reference rough cut with fixed shot order and picture timing. The manifest supplies shot durations, the times and identities of joins, available production-sound handles, an index of uncut dialogue takes, and an unaligned music window. These are candidate materials, not an assembled reference mix. Dialogue takes can contain surrounding speech, and some takes do not belong in the requested stretch. shot made for the trailer can arrive without production sound; the prompt and manifest identify such cases. The agent must deliver both output/edit.json and output/preview.mp4. The structured edit records the following choices: Dialogue: which supplied takes to use, the source-local in_s/out_s interval in each take, the output-timeline placement at_s, and any gain adjustment. Unneeded takes may be omitted; take may be reused when the edit calls for it. Production sound: whether to retain or mute shots own sound and, when handle is used, its source interval and timeline placement. Silent shots cannot supply production sound that does not exist. Music: the offset within the supplied cue that aligns with the start of the edit, and the resulting audible entry and balance. The agent must determine the alignment from the material. Every join: picture choice of cut, dip_to_black, dissolve, or other, and sound choice of hard, carries_over, prelap, or under. These respectively distinguish sound break, an L-cut, J-cut, and sound bridge. Every supplied join must be specified once; there is no quota requiring bridges or decorative transitions. Cards, when required by the task: text and appearance for supplied card placeholders. These are task-dependent, not requirement to add card to every stretch. The picture shots and their established timing remain fixed, subject to the requested join treatments. The rendered preview must make the declared choices audible and visible and stay within the duration allowance used by the submission validator. Merely declaring line in JSON does not establish that it can be heard in the final mix. The FC score combines judgment without the reference (weight 0.6) and reference-informed judgment (0.4); there is no deterministic exact-match component. The reference is one realized solution, and the rubrics evaluate task-appropriate alternatives through their actual audiovisual result. 22 A.5 Audit, Repair and Sampling We audit every constructed task with Gemini 3.8 Flash, giving it the task description, the available tools, the video and audio assets, and the hidden grading references. The audit checks whether the brief is supported by the supplied media and whether the grading rules evaluate decisions that can be inferred from the public input. For Content Selection and Narrative Sequencing it checks whether visual and narrative cues support the target selection or order. For Rough Cut and Fine Cut it checks the feasibility of the timing, dialogue and audiovisual requirements, and it allows several reasonable edits. Tasks with contradictory briefs, missing or corrupted assets, answer leakage, or unsupported reference constraints are repaired or dropped. repair makes targeted changes to prompts, references, graders or media, followed by file-integrity, decoding and grader checks as applicable. Unresolved tasks and incomplete audit responses leave the candidate pool. Review coverage varies, and some candidates receive additional independent-context reviews while others receive single audit or repair-author judgment. Filtering and repair leave 925 candidates. We draw 797 of them by fixed-seed sampling stratified by split, task type and film, which preserves film coverage within each type and uses no policy reward scores. The 128 unselected candidates remain valid and are set aside only to fix the dataset size and the type proportions. A.6 Split and Anti-Leakage Controls The initial construction uses film-level split: 43 films and 2,076 tasks in the training pool, and 6 films and 276 tasks in the validation pool. Filtering and sampling retain this film partition, yielding 716 training and 81 validation tasks. The 43 training films are 28 Years Later - The Bone Temple, Complete Unknown, Arthur the King, Avatar - The Way of Water, Ballerina, Beetlejuice Beetlejuice, Bugonia, Challengers, Crime 101, Dune - Part Two, Evil Dead Burn, Furious 7, His Three Daughters, Hit Man, Horizon - An American Saga - Chapter 1, How to Train Your Dragon, John Wick - Chapter 4, Land of Bad, Lee, M3GAN 2.0, Maria, May December, Mercy, Migration, Mission Impossible - The Final Reckoning, Mufasa - The Lion King, Oppenheimer, Ordinary Angels, Ricky Stanicky, Send Help, Smile 2, Song Sung Blue, The Bikeriders, The Hunger Games - The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, The Iron Claw, The Marvels, The Rip, The Wild Robot, Transformers One, Warfare, White Bird, Young Woman and the Sea, Zootopia 2. The 6 validation films are Deadpool & Wolverine, Heretic, Sinners, The Drama, They Will Kill You and Whiplash. Candidate identifiers are independently randomized across task types, competing clips share normalized encoding path, and answer records and reference alignments remain outside the policy-visible task package. Table 6 lists the final validation coverage. Filtering does not require every held-out film to contribute task of every type; for example, no Content Selection task from Deadpool & Wolverine is retained in this split. A.7 Example Tasks We expand the two worked task examples, Content Selection and Fine Cut, below and then provide additional Narrative Sequencing and Rough Cut examples. All four are actual validation tasks from the dataset used in our experiments. sections.title: B Editing Environment Details
sections.content: B.1 Episode State and Tools Each task runs in fresh filesystem workspace. The loader stages the task prompt, manifest, and only the media visible for the current task type. The public manifest identifies the supplied assets and the timing information appropriate to that task. Prepared frames and observation tools support Content Selection, Narrative Sequencing, and Rough Cut. Fine Cut additionally requires manipulation of the supplied picture, dialogue, production-sound and music assets to build an audiovisual timeline and render preview. Hidden answers, matching records, rubrics, and reference decisions remain in separate evaluator-owned directory. The policy may maintain notes, compare candidates, write timeline scripts, render intermediate results, inspect them, and revise its output. turn is one policy generation request; it may contain several tool calls, so turn count and tool-call count differ. The episode terminates when the policy produces final response or exhausts turn, context, or output budget. The common turn limit is 100. Termination by final response does not establish that valid deliverable exists or that the task has been completed successfully. B.2 Tools Beyond the harnesss own shell, which provides FFmpeg, ffprobe and Python for local cutting, joining, mixing and probing, the policy calls eight media tools over MCP. The policy interface supports text and images. The audio tools return analysis text rather than an audio waveform for the model to listen to. transcript may drop words, so the absence of transcript does not mean the absence of speech. The music tags come from read-only store built before training, not from an online model. Audio onsets and periodicity estimates are candidates for editing decisions, not guaranteed musical beats. The technical validator does not provide the hidden outcome score or certify artistic quality. Thus observation and validation tools can reduce uncertainty while still leaving the editing decision to the policy. B.3 Harness Episodes run in the official OpenCode harness at version 1.15.5, commit d7a6e1da. We do not modify its binary or its upstream source. The media tools above are served over MCP, and an image-registration plugin on the tool.execute.after hook intercepts both native image attachments and MCP image content, normalizing and registering each image before it reaches the conversation history. The recorded configuration also disables automatic compaction and pruning and retains the policys original generation inputs for replay. The plugin exists because the harness rearranges tool images into fresh user messages and may compress or trim history. Registering images ahead of that step keeps the request the inference backend receives identical to the one training replay reconstructs, so the policy is never optimized against pixels it did not see. Images that arrive by URL, in an unknown binary modality, or without registration are refused rather than silently downscaled or dropped. 30 Table 7: Media tools available to the policy. None of them exposes task label, hidden reference decision or an editing-specific oracle. Tool What it returns view_image inspect_video Prepared or policy-generated still images selected by path. Sampled video frames selected by timestamps or an interval; returns actual decoded times rather than continuous playback. inspect_frames Frame-index or time-based inspection near cut, optionally cropped; returns contact_sheet inspect_audio analyze_audio sheet or individual images. numbered sheet of up to 16 requested source images or frames. Duration, level, silence and an offline English transcript for requested audio window. Loudness, true peak, channel-level measurements, silence, and onset or pulse candidates for an audio window. validate_media Technical checks on declared edit or rendered file, including timing, stream/decode information and schema constraints. Pre-computed instrument, mood and energy descriptions for selected music window. listen_music B.4 Deliverable Validation At termination, the environment collects only the named deliverables: selection.json for Content Selection, order.json for Narrative Sequencing, cuts.json for Rough Cut, and edit.json together with preview.mp4 for Fine Cut. The submitted text response is not substitute for these artifacts. JSON validation checks types, identifiers, finite time values and the schema required by the task. Missing or malformed deliverables and violated submission constraints receive zero outcome reward. Infrastructure failures and unavailable grades are tracked separately rather than automatically counted as policy failures. Rough Cut checks. Every supplied clip must occur exactly once and in the supplied order. Each retained interval must have nonnegative in-point, an out-point after the in-point, and endpoints within the corresponding media. If the manifest specifies target duration , the sum of all retained intervals must be within max(1, min(3, 0.1T )) seconds of . This common delivery rule supersedes older total-duration tolerance text in the raw task prompt; it does not permit endpoints outside the source media. The original task-specific reference tolerances still define the separate deterministic quality metric (Appendix C.6). Fine Cut checks. The edit description must cover every supplied join exactly once. Picture join types are cut, dip_to_black, dissolve or other; sound relationships are hard, under, prelap or carries_over. Dialogue entries must reference available takes with valid trim intervals and placement times. Production sound must reference an existing source; explicit timing requires 31 supplied handle and all timing fields. Required title cards must be declared with nonempty text. declared music offset must lie inside the supplied cue. The preview must be probeable, contain video stream, and meet the same total-duration tolerance relative to the locked picture sequence. These structural checks do not by themselves prove that dialogue is intelligible, declared transition appears in the render, or the mix satisfies the brief; the outcome rubrics judge the actual delivered audiovisual result. B.5 Isolation and Telemetry Every trajectory executes in disposable sandbox without network access. Concurrent rollouts of the same task receive private workspaces, so one sample cannot inspect or overwrite another samples output. The environment logs turns, tool calls, images viewed, validation errors, rendering status, and reward components. These records support the later analysis of training cost, failure modes, and credit assignment without enlarging the policy-visible state. The same public task, observation tools and deliverable contract are used for student training rollouts and evaluation. Reward computations and OPSD teacher-only inputs are performed outside the policy sandbox. They do not enlarge the students public state or expose validation answers to it.

sections.title: C Training and Evaluation Details
sections.content: C.1 Training Configuration and Optimization Training configuration. Training uses asynchronous policy updates in SkyRL, with FSDP sharding and vLLM inference engines. Table 8 lists the settings shared by every training variant, and Table 9 lists the settings that differ. The periodic validation pass uses one rollout per task to monitor progress. Final reported scores use repeated evaluation of the selected final checkpoint; where available, its recorded validation pass supplies the first repetition and three additional passes complete avg@4. These repetitions vary rollout sampling, not the training seed. Policy optimization and advantage normalization. The reward-based variants use token-level importance ratios between the current policy and the rollout policy. Ratios outside (0.8, 1.28) receive zero weight; the retained ratios are treated as constants during backpropagation. The policy loss uses token-mean reduction over valid assistant tokens. For Equation 3.3, only valid process scores from turns with active loss tokens enter the group statistics, with ϵ = 106. The process advantage is zero for turns with missing or invalid scores, groups with fewer than two valid scores, or groups with sample standard deviation at most ϵ; the outcome term is retained. Process-weight schedule. The fixed variant uses λ = 0.5 at every update. For the decayed variant, the coefficient is 0.5 through update 20, then 0.5[1 (u 20)/10]3 for 20 < < 30, and zero from update 30 onward. Here is the consumer optimizers global update index, rather than the index at which an asynchronous rollout began. For example, updates 21 and 25 use coefficients 0.3645 and 0.0625. Setting the coefficient to zero removes the process term from the policy advantage; it does not change the outcome reward or the final evaluation grader. 32 Table 8: Training settings shared by all training variants. The token-mean loss divides the summed contributions of valid assistant tokens by the total number of such tokens in the optimization batch. Thus each valid token has the same reduction weight; turns and trajectories are not individually renormalized to have equal weight. Prompt tokens, tool observations, padding, and positions with an inactive loss mask do not contribute to this loss. The configured batch targets eight trajectories for each of 16 tasks in the reward-based variants and one trajectory for each of 16 tasks in each OPSD variant. Matching 50 updates therefore does not match the number of sampled trajectories or generated tokens across these objectives. The comparisons in this paper are comparisons of the specified training recipes. C.2 Process-Reward Judgments Context and timing. The process judge reviews consecutive windows of ten completed assistant turns; the final window may be shorter. It receives the original public task, public assistant actions and tool observations, registered images, and typed facts derived from the available records. Separate reasoning/thinking fields are excluded from this packet. Target turns and bounded selection of earlier turns retain detailed evidence; omitted earlier material is explicitly marked as incomplete history. The image packet prioritizes the current window and uses up to 16 original images, reserving at most four for earlier context. These are judge-input limits, not limits on the policys observations. Each window receives three independent judgments from Gemini 3.8 Flash. For particular turn, valid scores are averaged; an abstention is excluded from this average rather than treated as neutral vote. If no valid score remains, that turn receives no process contribution. The judge is asked to cite only evidence available at or before the turn being assessed. Since several target turns appear together in retrospective window, this citation rule does not establish that the models judgment is causally independent of later turns in that window. Table 10: Process-judgment decision rules. These summarize the implemented rubric; they specify intended supervision rather than guarantee the correctness of every judgment.

C.5 OPSD Teacher Inputs and Diagnostics Teacher and student. The KL teacher is frozen copy of the initial Qwen3.5-9B, initialized from the same checkpoint as the student. It is not updated by an exponential moving average or replaced by the trained student. The student samples its own actions from the public task context. Teacher-side privileged information changes the distribution evaluated at those same student action tokens; it is not inserted into student rollout or evaluation inputs, and it does not replace student actions with supervised action labels. Reference-answer conditioning. The private answer card contains the selected clip IDs for Content Selection; the reference order for Narrative Sequencing; and clip-relative reference in/out intervals and target duration for Rough Cut. For Fine Cut it contains reference join decisions, dialogue identities and onset times, and music source offset. The Fine Cut card is explicitly partial editing plan, not ready-to-submit executable edit: unprovided trim endpoints, gains, mixing envelopes and render commands are not invented as reference targets.
